Pre-market futures are rebounding modestly after a broad risk-off session. On the prior session the S&P 500 closed at 7683.69 (-0.77%), the Nasdaq Composite at 26820.38 (-0.92%), the Dow at 51481.51 (-0.67%) and the Russell 2000 at 2817.912 (-0.69%). This morning ES is 7755.75 (+0.12%), NQ is +0.25% and Dow futures are +0.12%. Oil is the biggest story: WTI is down 2.29% to 90.48 and Brent is down 2.05% to 103.12. Crude fell after Trump said US officials met Iran war mediators and after Saudi Arabia resumed exports through the East-West pipeline, although he has rejected Tehran's Hormuz reopening proposal. Europe is bid, with the Euro Stoxx 50 +0.77% and the STOXX 600 +0.46%. Bund yields are down 5.5bp to 3.588% and Gilt yields are down 6.6bp to 5.356%. US 2Y and 10Y yields are slightly lower at 4.9222% and 5.2299%, but the 30Y is up 1.36bp to 5.5602%, so the curve is steepening. Gold is up 0.88% to 4151.83. The VIX eased to 15.86. The warning sign is credit. US HY spreads widened 9bp to 3.03% and IG spreads widened 2bp to 0.82%, and spreads widened across EUR and EM too, even though spreads remain near historic tights. Sentiment is cautious rather than fearful: yields are high after the Fed's September hike, the index is stretched above trend, and positioning is crowded into tech.

“The oil dip buys the bulls a morning, but when credit widens while the VIX falls, something has to give.”

NY Harbor ULSD (US Diesel) — current: 467.00 cents/gal vs WTI

NY Harbor ULSD is at 467.0 cents/gal, the 99.8th percentile with a z-score of 3.14. The curve is in steep backwardation: the front month is 25.12 cents/gal over the 2nd month and 119.51 cents/gal over the 12th, and the crack spread is 105.55 $/bbl (z 5.86). Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

🔄Sector Analysis

The rotation is defensive and away from rate-sensitive cyclicals. On the prior session only Health Care (+0.29%), Consumer Staples (+0.40%) and Energy (+0.21%) rose in the US; the same three were the only gainers globally. Over one month the damage is broad in rate- and consumer-sensitive groups: US Utilities -8.69%, Real Estate -6.68%, Materials -6.72%, Financials -6.17%, Industrials -5.47% and Consumer Discretionary -5.18%. Only Communication Services (+3.80%), Info Tech (+3.04%) and Energy (+0.75%) are meaningfully higher. That split is the fingerprint of a 5.23% 10Y after a Fed hike: bond proxies are sold, and so are financials, down 3.0% over one week, possibly on funding and credit concerns. Meanwhile the AI/tech leadership keeps working, with US Info Tech +27.38% YTD and global Info Tech +34.32% YTD. Growth has beaten value on a one-month basis, but the prior session's tech (-0.70%) and communication services losses show the leadership is fragile. YTD, Energy (+35.85% US, +32.36% global) has been the other winner thanks to the war premium. Consumer Discretionary is negative YTD in both the US (-5.39%) and globally (-9.25%), which says the consumer is squeezed.

🧮Fixed Income Spreadscomputed

From the computed stats, credit is priced for perfection but starting to crack at the edges. US IG OAS is 0.82%, with a z-score of -0.77 and a 7th percentile rank; the historical minimum is 0.71% and the maximum 6.18%. It is 0 percentile against every crisis episode. US HY OAS is 3.03% (z -0.75, 16th percentile, 6th percentile of the 2022 hike episode). EUR IG is 0.90% (z -0.72, 19th percentile) and EUR HY is 3.10% (z -0.63, 20th percentile). EM USD OAS is 1.69% (z -1.30, 5th percentile), the richest of all. Every index widened today (HY +9bp, EUR HY +10bp, EM +5bp), while the VIX fell. Key levels, as analyst framing: IG 0.71% is the historical floor and cannot realistically be retested while financials are falling. IG 1.00% is a plausible first stop if Micron or another AI bellwether disappoints and the 10Y holds above 5.2%. IG 1.22%, the computed 2000-peak comparison level, requires an equity drawdown combined with a second Fed hike. HY 3.50% requires a spike in oil or Hormuz tensions and an equity pullback of more than 5%. HY 4.00% and above would take a growth scare that pushes the unemployment rate (4.1%) higher. On the tight side, HY back to 2.80% needs a verified Iran de-escalation and a pause from Warsh.

Widening velocity, not level. Near an all-time high a 63d widening past the trigger has historically raised P(SPX -10% within 3m) from ~8.6% to ~21.9% (Baa p=0.013, HY p=0.028, IG p=0.047, 1990-2026, corroborated on three independently-sourced series). The spread LEVEL carries no such signal once you control for already being in a drawdown (p=0.562) — tight spreads near a high are expected and are not reassurance. ARMED marks elevated tail RISK, not a sell: 78% of past ARMED episodes did not produce a 10% drawdown. 💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 48th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +78bp.

Latest reading is +1.41 vol points (97th percentile of the 30 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.51 (48th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), deteriorating over the past 3 months (+0.05 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.49pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +78bp (90th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 10bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +11bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 101.8 (74th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 108bp (steeper by 43bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Cup test

COMPONENTLEVELDATE
Left rim6.79%2000-01-20
Cup base0.51%2020-08-04
Right rim5.24%2026-09-28

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 75% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (93bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.24 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 75%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (39x) ≈ 22% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

This is a narrow, AI-led valuation bubble, not a broad mania. The S&P 500 CAPE is around 41, above 40 since May 2026, a level previously sustained only in the dot-com era. The Buffett indicator is about 237%, and the top 10 names are roughly 40% of the index. These are analyst estimates sourced from GuruFocus, BigGo and Motley Fool reports. The froth sits in semis: SOX at 92% of 2000 conditions matters most, since Micron reports this week at a $1.19T market cap. Unlike 2000, retail is bearish (AAII -15.4), margin-debt growth of 33.7% is under half the 2000 pace, and the Fed hiked into the rally rather than easing. The late-cycle catalysts that preceded the 2000 top (inverted curve, rolling PMIs) are absent. The bigger danger today is complacency in credit and volatility. Computed IG and Baa spreads are tighter than their 2000-peak comparison levels, which makes a credit-led repricing, not an earnings collapse, the more likely trigger for a correction. On the computed track, the current cycle anchored in Oct-2022 has reached 244.1 at month 47. That is above the 1990-anchored dot-com path at the same point (month 47 = 231.7) but far below its eventual peak.

⚔️Iran War

The conflict is in a tense diplomatic phase, with the Strait of Hormuz unresolved. On 2026-09-26, Trump rejected Tehran's proposal to reopen Hormuz within seven days (Al Jazeera). On 2026-09-27, the US disputed an Iranian claim that an 'advanced' drone had been seized in Hormuz. On 2026-09-28, Tehran warned it is 'fully prepared for war', while Trump said US officials had met Iran war mediators (Al Jazeera). Just Security's 2026-09-29 Early Edition reports that US officials say Trump is willing to offer sanctions relief and release frozen Iranian funds in exchange for concrete nuclear steps; Trump publicly called those reports 'untrue'. The same edition reports that US forces are completing their withdrawal from their last bases in Iraq, and that Saudi Arabia has resumed exports via the East-West pipeline after repairing drone-strike damage. That last point is the most direct explanation for this morning's oil drop (WTI -2.29%, Brent -2.05%). Fighting has also resumed in Yemen between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed government, with the WHO reporting more than 800 killed. Market read: talks lower tail risk at the margin, but Hormuz stays shut to normal traffic, so Brent's premium above $100 is only partly unwinding.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

At the September 16 FOMC, the Fed hiked 25bp to 3.75–4.00%, unanimously. It was the first hike since July 2023. In the dot plot, 12 of 18 participants see one more 25bp hike in 2026, four see 50bp more and two see none. Inference (not stated by Warsh): the next meeting is roughly a coin-flip-to-likely hike. Warsh said summer inflation readings 'do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved', and core PCE is still 3.34415%. Softer oil and cooling core-trend measures give him room to wait one meeting and hike in December instead. A hike is more likely if Brent stays above $100 and the next core PCE print holds above 3%.

~1 YEAR

Inference from his on-record statements: a funds rate around 4.00–4.25% after one or two more hikes, followed by an extended hold rather than quick cuts. That is paired with a continued push to shrink the balance sheet and narrow the Fed's footprint, the 'regime change' agenda CNBC reports is meeting internal resistance. Cuts in the next year likely require core PCE clearly heading toward 2.5% or a credit or growth shock. The 2Y yield at 4.9222% already sits well above the current target range, which is consistent with markets pricing a higher-for-longer path.

Warsh has framed the Fed's job as delivering price stability and a 'timelier return' to 2%. He has asserted Fed independence (KPMG) and has long argued for a smaller balance sheet and less forward guidance. His July hold was paired with price-stability language, and September delivered the hike. The flagged inference is that he prefers acting early to being late on inflation, and that he will use balance-sheet policy alongside rates, which adds upward pressure on long-end yields (30Y 5.5602%, rising today). For markets, that is headwind for rate-sensitive sectors (Utilities -8.69% over one month) and for long-duration equity multiples.
